title: Having Children
note: The twice-born owe three debts: to the sages, paid by study, to the gods, paid by sacrifice, and to the ancestors, paid only by begetting sons. This chapter is about having children to pay that debt.

couplets.plain: Of all that can be gained, we know of nothing else like children with understanding.
couplets.pm: Among all a man can gain, we value no gain but sons fit to know what should be known. “With understanding” shows that the word for children here leaves out daughters. The past tense is used because a fit nature is sure to bring knowledge. This tells the excellence of having sons.
couplets.sensitive: Could hurt someone who is childless.

links.reason: Puts children with understanding above every other gain.

couplets.plain: In all seven births, evils won’t touch you if you have children of good character, free of blame.
couplets.pm: In all seven births that deeds bring, suffering won’t reach a man who has sons of good qualities that no one blames. His bad deeds wear away through the gifts and righteous acts such sons perform for their parents, and their good qualities are the cause of those acts. The seven births are the seven kinds of being.

links.quote: children of good character, free of blame

couplets.plain: People say their children are their wealth. That wealth comes by each one’s own deeds.
couplets.pm: The wise call a man’s sons his wealth, because what those sons earn comes to him through the good deeds they do for his sake. Sons who earn are called wealth as a manner of speaking. These two couplets tell the reward of good sons in the next life.

links.quote: People say their children are their wealth
links.reason: Calls children wealth, and ties that wealth to their own deeds.

couplets.plain: Sweeter by far than ambrosia is the porridge your own children have stirred with their small hands.
couplets.pm: Rice mixed by the small hands of your own children tastes far sweeter than ambrosia. To mix it is to drop it, touch it, bite it, stir it and scatter the ghee-soaked food over themselves.

links.quote: your own children have stirred with their small hands
links.reason: A child’s mess in a bowl of porridge beats ambrosia itself.
Uses ambrosia as the sweetness that simple porridge outdoes.

couplets.plain: Touching your children’s bodies is joy to the body, and hearing their words is joy to the ear.
couplets.pm: The body’s joy is touching your children’s bodies, and the ear’s joy is hearing their words. “Words” is left general because what they say once they are learned is a joy too, not only their baby talk.

links.quote: Touching your children’s bodies is joy to the body

couplets.plain: “The flute is sweet, the harp is sweet,” say those who have not heard the babble of their own children.
couplets.pm: Those who haven’t heard the lisping words of their own sons say the music of the flute and the harp is sweet. Those who have heard them would call those words sweeter. These three couplets tell the reward of children in this life.

links.quote: the babble of their own children

couplets.plain: The good a father does his son is to put him in the front rank of the assembly.
couplets.pm: The good a father does his son is to make him so learned that he stands above others in the assembly of the learned. Making him rich and the like isn’t good, because that brings suffering. This tells the father’s duty.

links.quote: in the front rank of the assembly
links.reason: Sets the goal of raising a son: to see him at the front of the assembly.

links.quote: The good a father does his son
to put him in the front rank

couplets.plain: That your children know more than you is sweet to every living being on this great earth.
couplets.pm: Your children’s understanding is sweeter to all those on this great earth than it is to you. Understanding here means learning joined to natural intelligence. “Living beings” means the wise, since only they can delight in seeing it. So the assembly rejoices even more than the father.
couplets.note: தம்மின், “than oneself”, can go with the children’s understanding, as here. He joins it to “sweet”: their understanding is sweeter to the world than to the parent.

links.quote: is sweet to every living being
links.reason: Calls children’s greater understanding a joy to every living being.

links.quote: your children know more than you
That your children know more than you

couplets.plain: A mother who hears her son called a man of worth feels more joy than when she bore him.
couplets.pm: A mother who hears the wise call her son complete in learning rejoices more than at the time she bore him. A mother’s joy in her child has no measure, so it is told on its own here.

links.quote: hears her son called a man of worth
A mother who hears her son

couplets.plain: What a son does in return for his father is to make people say, “What penance did his father do to have him?”
couplets.pm: The return a son makes to the father who had him taught is to live so that people who see his understanding and conduct say, “What penance did his father do to get him?” This tells the son’s duty.

links.quote: What penance did his father do to have him?
What a son does in return for his father
